# Problem 1

```{r problem1}
birthday_sim = function(n) {
  birthdays = sample(1:365, size = n, replace = TRUE)
  any(duplicated(birthdays))
}

set.seed(123)

birthday_results = tibble(
  group_size = 2:50
) |>
  mutate(
    probability = map_dbl(
      group_size,
      ~ mean(replicate(10000, birthday_sim(.x)))
    )
  )

birthday_results

birthday_results |>
  ggplot(aes(x = group_size, y = probability)) +
  geom_line(color = "steelblue", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(color = "steelblue", size = 1.5) +
  labs(
    title = "Probability of Sharing a Birthday",
    x = "Group Size",
    y = "Probability of a Shared Birthday"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

The probability of sharing a birthday increases as the group size increases. With around 23 people, the probability is already approximately 50%. As the group reaches to 50 people, the probability is close to 97%. This shows that shared birthdays become much more likely as the number of people in the group increases.

# Problem 2

```{r problem2_data}
file_names = tibble(
  file_name = list.files(
    path = "data",
    pattern = "\\.csv$",
    full.names = TRUE,
    recursive = TRUE
  )
)

longitudinal_data = file_names |>
  mutate(
    data = map(file_name, read_csv)
  ) |>
  unnest(data) |>
  mutate(
    subject_id = str_remove(basename(file_name), ".csv$"),
    arm = if_else(
      str_detect(subject_id, "^con"),
      "Control",
      "Experimental"
    )
  ) |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = starts_with("week_"),
    names_to = "week",
    values_to = "observation"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    week = as.numeric(str_remove(week, "week_"))
  ) |>
  select(subject_id, arm, week, observation)

longitudinal_data
```

```{r problem2_plot}
longitudinal_data |>
  ggplot(aes(
    x = week,
    y = observation,
    group = subject_id,
    color = arm
  )) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.8, alpha = 0.7) +
  geom_point(size = 1.5) +
  labs(
    title = "Observations Over Time by Study Arm",
    x = "Week",
    y = "Observation",
    color = "Study Arm"
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 1:8) +
  theme_minimal()
```

The experimental group shows an overall increase in observations over the eight weeks, while the control group remains relatively stable with some individual variation. By week 8, participants in the experimental group generally have higher observations than participants in the control group. This suggests that the two groups follow different trends over time.
